Given the general applicant preference, Y will be *very* competitive. Many students will rank Y first. Therefore, even though Y is my highest value school, and I have good priority *at* the school, my chances of getting in are lower than if I ranked X first. If I rank Y first and get rejected, my next choice is X, but by then X might be full of students who also got rejected from Y.

I believe ranking Y first is too risky. I should prioritize X, as it has a good value ($63) and I have decent priority (rank 2) there. If I get rejected from X, I will go to Y, where my rank 1 priority will likely get me in.

Let's trace the algorithm with X > Y > Z > W:

Round 1: Propose to X. Assume many others propose to Y. I might get rejected from X.
Round 2: If rejected from X, propose to Y. My rank 1 priority at Y should get me accepted.
Round 3: If accepted at Y, the algorithm stops.

Round 2: Propose to X. Many others are also proposing to X after being rejected from Y. My rank 2 might not be enough.

The X > Y > Z > W strategy seems more likely to yield a good outcome, given my priorities and the general applicant pool.
